objective: Matching a requirements-gathering technique to a scenario: user stories, use cases, stakeholder interviews, surveys, workshops, and lessons learned

sources.cite: PMI, Certified Associate in Project Management (CAPM) Examination Content Outline, 2023 Exam Update: Fundamentals and Core Concepts 36%, Predictive Plan-Based Methodologies 17%, Agile Frameworks/Methodologies 20%, Business Analysis Frameworks 27%
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 through a summarizing fetch of a copy of PMI's PDF hosted by a university. Relevant text: Domain 1 Task 5 'Demonstrate an understanding of common problem-solving tools and techniques' ('Evaluate the effectiveness of a meeting'; 'Explain the purpose of focus groups, standup meetings, brainstorming, etc.'); Domain 2 Task 2 ('Apply critical path methods'; 'Calculate schedule variance') and Task 3 ('Calculate cost and schedule variances'). The objective wording here is the course seed's. Reused for REQ-336 from this course's sprint-status-meeting-daily-scrum-capm (the same reading and date); the objective wording is the course seed's.
The organization, the project and the people are fictional. The minutes or days each step takes and the effects of each decision are teaching simplifications for exam practice, not measured values.

brief.situation: You are the business analyst on a fictional app for the Riverbend public library system: patrons will book study rooms and equipment. Twelve branches, 40 staff and 30,000 patrons.
handover: The branches book rooms differently today.
A similar app at another library failed because staff found it slower than paper.
howItWorks: The board shows the risk register against the appetite, each stakeholder's support in words and the docket.
Move on a week at a time. A decision comes to you at each review; before the first, you can read the evidence.
At the end you write the record and a short reflection.

effects.finding: Staff were never observed at the desk; booking took longer than paper; rules differed by branch and the app ignored them.

then.log: Week 2: branch managers refuse to pilot an app that ignores their rules; the sponsor delays the launch.
Week 3: the prototype takes four minutes for a phone booking; staff vote to keep paper.
Week 4: accessibility advocates find the booking screens unusable with screen readers; launch is blocked.

staffPrompt.title: Twelve branches, twelve rule sets
staffPrompt.context: Branch managers disagree on booking limits.

choices.label: Run a facilitated workshop with the twelve branch managers to agree common booking rules and the allowed local variations

effects.log: Common rules are agreed with two local variations.

choices.feedback: Workshops bring stakeholders with conflicting needs together to reach agreement efficiently.

choices.label: Interview each manager separately
choices.feedback: Detailed, but the conflicts are never resolved together.

choices.label: Adopt the main branch's rules for everyone

deskPrompt.title: How staff really book today
deskPrompt.context: The other library's app failed at the desk.

choices.label: Interview and observe front-desk staff at three branches during busy hours, and write use cases for desk bookings, checking them against the lessons learned

effects.log: Desk use cases capture a 30-second phone booking.

choices.feedback: Interviews and observation reveal how work is really done; lessons learned point to where the last project failed.

choices.label: Write desk requirements from the managers' description
choices.feedback: Managers describe the process as it should be, not as it is.

choices.label: Skip desk staff; patrons will book online
choices.feedback: Phone and walk-in bookings, a third of today's, have no design.

choices.label: Send a short survey to patrons in English and Spanish, with accessible formats, and turn the findings into user stories with acceptance criteria
choices.feedback: Surveys gather input from large groups; user stories with acceptance criteria carry their needs into the backlog.

choices.label: Interview ten patrons who visit the main branch
choices.feedback: Useful depth, but ten main-branch patrons do not represent 30,000.

choices.label: Write patron stories from the team's own experience
choices.feedback: The team's needs are not patrons' needs; accessibility needs are missed.

scoring.modelReasoning: Match the technique to the situation: workshops reconcile conflicting stakeholders, interviews and observation show how work is really done, surveys reach large groups, lessons learned point to past failures, and use cases and user stories carry the needs into design.
